Through SAE pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, we build SlideOn from DenseOn and mSlideOn from mLateOn, reusing their existing retrieval knowledge to learn sparse representations compatible with efficient inverted-index search. SlideOn reaches 56.68 on BEIR-15, surpassing DenseOn’s 56.20, and uses sparse vector pruning to achieve leading performance on the search and storage efficiency Pareto frontiers among sub-2B models. mSlideOn supports multilingual, long-context, and code retrieval, outperforming mDenseOn by +4.76 points on multilingual retrieval (MIRACL) and +10.19 points on long-document retrieval (MLDR), while also surpassing mLateOn and mDenseOn on code retrieval (MTEB Code). mSlideOn brings the multilingual and long-context strengths of late interaction to efficient sparse retrieval, with strong generalization beyond its retrieval training languages. With Matryoshka-style training, both models maintain strong retrieval performance as pruning increases, allowing users to adjust them to fit their latency and storage budgets. As we always do, we release the SAE checkpoints, fine-tuned retrieval models, and training code under a permissive license to support further research. Get started now: 🗂️ Collection: SlideOn & mSlideOn 🌐 Multilingual model: mSlideOn 🔤 English model: SlideOn 🧩 SAE pretrained checkpoints: SlideOn-SAE | mSlideOn-SAE 📚 Training data: EN | FR | ES | IT | DE | PT | AR | NO | SV | Code | Code Edit 🛠️ Training and evaluation scripts: slideon-mslideon Introduction Over the past few months, we released DenseOn and LateOn , our open dense and late-interaction models for English retrieval, then extended our recipe to multilingual, long-context and code retrieval to build mDenseOn and mLateOn . These releases validated our data recipe and training setup while enabling a controlled comparison of single-vector and multi-vector retrieval under a matched setup. Alongside this work, we explored how to regularize late-interaction models to work better with efficient ANN indexes such as SMVE/MUVERA ( LateOn-regularized ) and how to reduce its inference costs via hierarchical pooling training ( LateOn-hpool-regularized ). The limitations of dense and late-interaction retrievers led us to take a closer look at sparse retrieval, a direction we had not yet explored in depth. Sparse retrieval represents each query and document as a vector in which most values are zero. The remaining nonzero are positive values and assign weights to a small set of features that we call latents, which may represent vocabulary terms or learned concepts. Sparse encoding pipeline. Contextualized token embeddings are projected into sparse latent vectors, then max-pooled across tokens to produce a single query or document representation. Concept labels are illustrative. An inverted index stores, for each latent, a list of documents where that latent was activated, called posting-lists . Search can then focus only on documents that share active latents with the query without scanning the entire corpus. This property can be particularly valuable for large collections, where reducing the amount of data accessed per query enables efficient search across billions of documents. Sparse retrieval pipeline with an inverted index. Each latent’s posting list stores document identifiers and weights. Active query latents select the lists to traverse, and query–document weight products are accumulated into document scores. Documents sharing no active latents with the query are skipped. Concept labels and weights are illustrative. The SPLADE family ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ) has long demonstrated that learned sparse retrieval (LSR) enables semantic matching with efficient inverted-index search. In SPLADE models, each vector component corresponds to a vocabulary term (“dog”, “cat”, “cow”), so the model learns vocabulary weights and which additional terms to activate beyond those present in the input tokens. This expansion helps address the vocabulary mismatch that affects lexical methods such as BM25, allowing related wording such as “car” and “automobile” to match. The resulting representations retain interpretable term weights while supporting compact indexes and low retrieval latency. LACONIC demonstrates that sparse retrievers running index search on CPU can achieve superior quality with similar latency compared to dense baselines that rely on GPUs for fast search, which are the industry standard now. They also show that depending on document sparsity, sparse retrieval can use substantially less index memory than dense vectors. In parallel, more recent work highlights the value of sparse representations for accelerating multi-vector retrieval. SMVE uses sparse representations to retrieve candidates before full late-interaction reranking, while SSR uses sparse coding and inverted indexes to replace expensive k-means clustering in multi-vector retrieval. Beyond these efficiency benefits, sparse representations may also offer advantages for long-context retrieval by easing the compression bottleneck of encoding an entire document into a single low-dimensional dense vector, as discussed here . SPARSEUP is a notable recent contribution that pushes the frontier of retrieval quality and efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art BEIR-13 results under 150M parameters while supporting sub-millisecond index search on MS MARCO with the SEISMIC efficient sparse index. Built over LateOn-unsupervised checkpoint and trained on our open English fine-tuning mixture , it demonstrates how existing checkpoints and data can be reused to train competitive sparse retrievers. These results encouraged us to build on our previous work and investigate how to convert dense and late-interaction models into efficient state-of-the-art sparse retrievers. Recent studies demonstrate that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used as effective initialization for sparse retrievers. SAE-SPLADE demonstrates that SPLADE’s MLM-initialized sparse vocabulary can be replaced with a learned latent vocabulary while maintaining comparable retrieval performance. The latent vocabulary is learned through SAE pretraining, then fine-tuned with the backbone for retrieval. SPLARE explores the same principle with LLM backbones, reusing publicly available pretrained SAEs and fine-tuning only the backbone. It achieves results competitive with state-of-the-art dense retrievers, alongside strong cross-lingual generalization. Latent Terms shows that effective sparse retrieval features compatible with BM25 can be extracted from trained dense and late-interaction models with SAE training only. PUMA explores a supervised approach for multimodal embeddings, combining SAE reconstruction with retrieval fine-tuning of the sparse vocabulary while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Compared with sparse representations learned from a tokenizer vocabulary, these SAE-learned latent vocabularies offer some advantages. Features can capture shared concepts across different expressions, distinguish different meanings of an ambiguous word, and align semantically related content across languages. Their dimensionality can also be chosen independently of the tokenizer vocabulary, giving more flexibility over representational capacity. These advantages motivated us to explore SAEs as a way to convert existing dense and late-interaction representations into sparse features while reusing their learned retrieval knowledge. SAE pretraining and supervised fine-tuning are computationally much cheaper than large-scale retrieval pretraining, and the community now offers a large collection of openly released dense models alongside a growing set of strong late-interaction models. In this work, we therefore explore how to convert our matched late-interaction and dense retrievers into efficient learned sparse retrievers (LSRs) through SAE pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, building on their existing representations and our validated data recipe. Training Data We reuse our multilingual supervised fine-tuning data released with mDenseOn and mLateOn . We prioritize comparability with our dense and late-interaction models over broader language and script coverage, keeping the same training data and teacher distillation setup. The mixture contains about 16.3M query-positive pairs across nine natural languages and code. Most multilingual examples come from translations of our curated English datasets, supplemented with native multilingual supervision from only 4 of MIRACL’s 16 training language splits: Arabic, English, French, and Spanish. The mixture also includes long-document pairs from 7 of MLDR’s 13 training language splits and code retrieval data from LateOn-Code and CodeEditSearchTrain. Per-dataset language mix and total number of query-positive pairs in the filtered contrastive fine-tuning data. In this dataset, each query-positive pair contains 10 mined hard negatives. The positive and negative documents are annotated with relevance scores from the mxbai-rerank-large-v2 cross-encoder, providing teacher supervision for retrieval training. For English-only models, we select the English splits of this mixture. Sparse Autoencoder Pretraining Our initial goal was to convert our trained dense and late-interaction models into sparse retrievers by training only an SAE on their frozen representations, following Latent Terms. However, we found that explicitly optimizing these sparse representations for retrieval could bring substantial improvements, as we show in our SAE/SFT ablations . We therefore use SAE pretraining to learn an initial latent dictionary before adapting it through supervised sparse retrieval fine-tuning. An SAE learns to reconstruct dense vectors using a small number of learned features. We train ours on individual L2-normalized token embeddings, using dense 768-dimensional or late-interaction 128-dimensional unpooled token representations. We justify our choice of backbone and auxiliary loss in our dense versus LI ablations , which compare their effects on reconstruction, latent usage, downstream retrieval performance, and search efficiency. Supervised Fine-Tuning for Sparse Retrieval During SFT, we discard the SAE decoder and train only the backbone and the sparse encoder. Following SAE setup, each normalized token embedding is mapped to a sparse vector with 32,768 latents using top-32 latent pooling followed by ReLU. We then apply latent-wise max pooling across tokens to obtain a single sparse representation for each query or document. Unlike prior approaches that apply log ⁡ ( 1 + z ) \log(1+z) lo g ( 1 + z ) to latent activations, we retain their original magnitudes and compute retrieval scores with a raw dot product. We find that omitting this transformation improves retrieval performance when applying pruning to the final sparse vectors. We combine the InfoNCE contrastive loss with KL-divergence distillation from cross-encoder scores, matching the mDenseOn/mLateOn setup. We apply Matryoshka training to both losses over pruned query–document pairs to support flexible sparsity at inference, as demonstrated in our SlideOn results section . Pruning retains only the top-n latents with the largest activation values in each final pooled vector. For SlideOn , we retain 32, 64, or 128 query latents and 512 or 1024 document latents. For mSlideOn , we retain 128 or 256 query latents and 512, 1024, or 2048 document latents. We train on all pair-wise combinations for each model. We train SlideOn with a batch size of 128 and mSlideOn with a batch size of 512, both using 7 mined hard negatives and in-batch negatives. We use a contrastive temperature of 0.02 and for KL distillation, we use a student temperature of 0.02 and a teacher temperature of 1. We retain the load-balancing objective, averaging its query and document terms equally, to keep the number of dead latents low during retrieval fine-tuning. We further add FLOPS regularization terms for the pooled query and document vectors. We find that FLOPS regularization improves training stability with dot-product scoring, despite producing only small changes in overall sparsity, which is mainly controlled by top-k mechanism. We hypothesize that penalizing large average activations encourages the model to allocate weight more selectively to latents that contribute to retrieval. To improve both retrieval efficiency and index storage, we prune the final query and document sparse vectors by keeping only their $n$ largest activations. Query pruning directly increases search efficiency because fewer posting lists need to be consulted, while document pruning reduces the length of posting lists, improving search efficiency and reducing the memory required to store documents in the index. With documents pruned to the top-512 latents (d-512) and query budgets ranging from full vectors to the top-32 latents (q-32), SlideOn lies on the quality-efficiency frontier among the compared sub-2B models. Similarly, with unpruned queries and document budgets ranging from full vectors to the top-128 latents (d-128), SlideOn lies on the quality-storage cost frontier among compared models. We trained SlideOn with a Matryoshka-style setup during SFT to concentrate retrieval information in the strongest query and document latents, limiting the performance drop under aggressive pruning. As shown below, this setup better preserves retrieval performance as query or document pruning increases. Although it comes with a small drop in unpruned performance, we chose to retain the Matryoshka setup for its better quality-efficiency tradeoff under pruning. Prioritizing the strongest latents also helps limit weak or unhelpful latents, reducing retrieval FLOPS even with unpruned query vectors (q-full). SlideOn with Matryoshka versus standard training. The left panel varies query pruning with unpruned documents; the right varies document pruning with unpruned queries. Matryoshka training better preserves retrieval quality under stronger pruning. FLOPS and document NNZ are measured on SciFact, NFCorpus, and FiQA. Multilingual Retrieval: mSlideOn We follow the same evaluation protocol as for the English models, running exact search over each full evaluation corpus and scoring pairs with dot product and unpruned query/document vectors. Alongside BEIR-15 for English retrieval, we evaluate multilingual retrieval on MIRACL, long-context retrieval on MLDR, and code retrieval on MTEB Code. Since our supervised retrieval training mixture covers a limited set of languages, we report both target-language (tgt) and full-benchmark scores for MIRACL and MLDR, following the mDenseOn and mLateOn. Target scores average performance over benchmark languages included in our training mixture, while full scores cover all benchmark languages, including those absent from retrieval fine-tuning. This lets us assess performance on training languages alongside broader multilingual generalization. Model Params. Open s. multilingual corresponds to opensearch-neural-sparse-encoding-multilingual-v1. The most controlled comparison is with mDenseOn and mLateOn, since we use the same backbone, supervised training data, and cross-encoder distillation setup. We also include other sparse, dense, and late-interaction baselines to position mSlideOn against the broader state of the art. On English retrieval measured on BEIR-15, mSlideOn reaches 56.00 , the strongest result among the multilingual sparse models in our comparison. Its performance remains relatively close to mDenseOn at 56.70, while trailing mLateOn at 57.56. On multilingual retrieval measured on MIRACL target languages (en, fr, es, de, ar), mSlideOn achieves 63.21 , improving on mDenseOn by +3.60 points and remaining competitive with strong baselines such as pplx-embed-v1-0.6b at 63.18, while still trailing mLateOn at 65.61. On full MIRACL (18 languages), mSlideOn reaches 62.78 , improving on mDenseOn by +4.76 points , while still trailing mLateOn at 67.04 and other baselines that were explicitly trained on many more languages. The improvements over mDenseOn show that sparse retrieval can outperform dense models across diverse multilingual retrieval tasks . Our training data covers only 4 training splits (Arabic, English, French, and Spanish) of the 18 MIRACL's languages. By comparison, BGE-M3 and MILCO use MIRACL training data spanning 16 languages. This broader supervision provides context for their stronger performance. On long-document retrieval evaluated on MLDR, mSlideOn reaches 75.79 on target languages (en, fr, es, de, ar, it, pt) and 61.68 on the full benchmark (13 languages), strongly improving on mDenseOn by +10.17 and +10.18 points, respectively, while still trailing mLateOn at 87.68/77.92. On MLDR, mSlideOn outperforms every dense baseline in our comparison, including models explicitly trained with MLDR data such as Qwen3-Embedding, mGTE and BGE-M3, which is consistent with prior findings that sparse representations can be more effective than pooled dense embeddings for long-context retrieval . Among other baselines, it trails mGTE on both language sets and BGE-M3 sparse on the full languages, which is expected since these models are broadly trained on MDLR data, whereas our mixture restricts MLDR supervision to only 7 target languages. Perhaps the most surprising result is on code retrieval evaluated on MTEB Code. mSlideOn reaches 74.78 , outperforming every compared sparse and late-interaction baseline , including mLateOn at 73.48. It also remains competitive with the strongest dense baselines that do not disclose their training data. This demontrates the strong potential of sparse models for code retrieval tasks . The detailed per-task and per-language performance gaps can be seen below, showing that mSlideOn outperforms mDenseOn on most evaluated tasks and languages, while still trailing mDenseOn on particular BEIR-15 tasks. Per-dataset and per-language differences in nDCG@10 points for mSlideOn versus mDenseOn. Teal bars indicate gains and red bars indicate declines relative to mDenseOn. Blue labels mark languages included in retrieval training. Contributions of SAE Pretraining and Supervised Retrieval Fine-Tuning We found that supervised retrieval fine-tuning can substantially improve performance over SAE pretraining alone. To assess the contribution of each stage, we compare four configurations. SAE only trains the SAE on frozen backbone representations, while SFT only trains the sparse retriever without SAE pretraining using our token-sampling initialization. SAE → SFT uses SAE pretraining to initialize the sparse encoder before retrieval fine-tuning. Finally, SAE + SFT jointly optimizes the SAE reconstruction and supervised retrieval objectives within a single training stage. We additionally evaluate SPARSEUP SFT under the same training data, distillation, backbone model, and top-32 pooling to compare its MLM-based setup with our methods. As shown below, SAE → SFT achieves the highest BEIR-15 score, motivating our choice of sequential SAE pretraining followed by SFT. SPARSEUP SFT yields the lowest retrieval FLOPS among the evaluated configurations, with slightly reduced retrieval performance. This trade-off suggests that its MLM-based initialization is promising for ultra-sparse retrieval setups. Bold values indicate the best result for each metric. Models are trained over DenseOn. SAE only uses BM25 scoring, following Latent Terms. SAE + SFT uses a reconstruction loss weight of 0.1. Models were not trained with our Matryoshka top-n pruning formulation. Dense and Late-Interaction Initialization for Sparse Retrieval We compare sparse retrievers initialized from dense and late-interaction models to understand how the starting representations affect sparse retrieval and to choose the best setups for SlideOn and mSlideOn. We study both DenseOn and LateOn, alongside their multilingual counterparts, mDenseOn and mLateOn. A strictly controlled comparison is difficult because their token embedding spaces differ substantially in dimensionality and geometry. With a sparse latent space of D = 32 , 768 D = 32,768 D = 32 , 768 , a direct linear encoder projection requires 768 x 32,768 weights (25.2M) for our dense models, compared with 128 x 32,768 (4.2M) for our late-interaction models. Randomly sampled dense token embeddings also have substantially lower cosine similarity than late-interaction embeddings (0.175 for DenseOn vs. 0.959 for LateOn on FiQA). In our experiments, the spatial anisotropy makes it harder for the SAE to learn accurate reconstructions. As explained in the SAE section, we address these differences through centered dictionary initialization and a more complex encoder to increase capacity for late-interaction models. A recurring observation is that our sparse models initialized from late interaction produce higher dead-latent rates during both SAE pretraining and SFT. We observe that without sufficient control, latent usage can collapse onto a small subset of the encoder dictionary, reducing effective representational capacity and increasing retrieval FLOPS. In our experiments, starting from LateOn SAE and adding the load-balancing loss during SFT reduces the proportion of dead latents from 54.85% to 0.128%. Starting from DenseOn SAE, it reduces retrieval FLOPS from 57.02 to 52.89 while slightly improving BEIR-15 nDCG@10 from 56.73 to 57.03, highlighting the benefits of directly incentivizing broader latent usage during SFT. These findings led us to explore load balancing during SAE pretraining as a potential replacement for the AuxK loss. Nevertheless, AuxK pretraining yields slightly better English retrieval performance and lower FLOPS for both initializations. These results suggest that encouraging broader latent usage during SAE pretraining without jointly optimizing a retrieval objective may, in some cases, slightly reduce downstream retrieval quality and increase retrieval FLOPS. For English retrieval, DenseOn initilization outperforms LateOn on BEIR-15 under both auxiliary losses, with a small quality advantage and lower retrieval FLOPS. These results motivate our choice of DenseOn AuxK SAE as the initialization for SlideOn. The multilingual models show a different pattern from the English-only experiments, with load balancing offering a more favorable trade-off between retrieval quality and FLOPS. As shown below, load-balancing eliminates dead latents during SAE pretraining for both backbones. For mDenseOn, it preserves reconstruction quality and slightly improves retrieval across all four benchmarks, with a modest increase in FLOPS from 59.01 to 63.75. For mLateOn, it strongly reduces FLOPS from 76.47 to 53.05 while maintaining broadly comparable retrieval performance . These findings support an advantage of load balancing during SAE pretraining for multilingual retrieval. Comparing the two initializations, mDenseOn achieves sligthly better English (BEIR-15) and code retrieval (MTEB Code) scores, while mLateOn performs substantially better on multilingual (MIRACL) and long-document retrieval (MLDR). These advantages mirror mLateOn’s strengths over mDenseOn, including stronger multilingual generalization, especially to languages absent from retrieval fine-tuning, and better long-document retrieval. This suggests that sparse retrievers initialized from late-interaction checkpoints inherit these properties, even if they do not fully match the retrieval performance of their late-interaction initialization in our setup. These results motivate our choice of mLateOn load-balance SAE as the initialization for mSlideOn. Conclusion In this work, we show that existing dense and late-interaction checkpoints can be converted into effective sparse retrievers through SAE pretraining and supervised retrieval fine-tuning, both substantially cheaper than large-scale retrieval pretraining. SlideOn improves over DenseOn on BEIR-15 and uses sparse vector pruning to achieve leading performance on both the quality–search cost and quality–storage cost Pareto frontiers among the compared sub-2B models. mSlideOn improves over mDenseOn in multilingual, long-document, and code retrieval, including languages absent from retrieval fine-tuning. These results highlight the potential of sparse retrievers to replace dense models while maintaining strong retrieval quality and enabling inverted-index search. Our ablations show that the choice of backbone and SAE setup matters. DenseOn with AuxK provides the best English initialization in our experiments, while mLateOn with load balancing offers a stronger foundation for posterior multilingual fine-tuning. Matryoshka training complements these choices by preserving retrieval quality under pruning, allowing query and document sparsity to be adjusted at inference without retraining. Future work can expand supervision to more languages and scripts, further investigate how to better preserve late-interaction matching capabilities during sparsification, and improve the SAE setup. We release our SAE checkpoints, fine-tuned retrieval models, and training scripts to enable further research. SlideOn

English Sparse Retrieval Model by LightOn

SlideOn | mSlideOn | SlideOn-SAE | mSlideOn-SAE

> 🎯 TL;DR: A 174M-parameter English sparse retrieval model built from DenseOn through sparse autoencoder (SAE) pretraining and supervised retrieval fine-tuning. SlideOn reaches 56.68 nDCG@10 on BEIR-15, surpassing DenseOn's 56.20, while producing sparse representations compatible with inverted-index search. Joint query/document Matryoshka training preserves retrieval quality under pruning, allowing search and storage costs to be adjusted at inference without retraining. ## About the SlideOn / mSlideOn Family With [DenseOn and LateOn](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon), then [mDenseOn and mLateOn](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon), we explored dense and late-interaction retrieval using our open data recipe. SlideOn and mSlideOn reuse these models' retrieval knowledge to learn sparse representations through SAE pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. SlideOn starts from [DenseOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn) for English retrieval. [mSlideOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mSlideOn) starts from [mLateOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn) for multilingual, long-context, and code retrieval. We release both the pretrained SAE initializations and the final retrieval models. See our [blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/slideon-mslideon) for the full method, results, and ablations. ## SlideOn SlideOn encodes queries and documents into 32,768-dimensional nonnegative sparse vectors. A learned linear encoder maps each normalized DenseOn token representation to its top-32 latent activations, followed by ReLU. Max pooling across tokens produces one vector per query or document, and retrieval uses the dot product between these vectors. The dimensions are learned features, independent of the tokenizer vocabulary. Active latents can be stored in an inverted index, where query latents select posting lists and their weights contribute to document scores. SlideOn notably: - Reaches 56.68 on BEIR-15 with unpruned vectors, improving on DenseOn by 0.48 points. - Reaches 56.98 with unpruned queries and documents capped at 512 nonzero latents. - Retains 56.66 with queries capped at 64 and documents at 512, reducing the measured retrieval FLOPS proxy to 8.72. - Supports inputs of up to 8,192 tokens and independently adjustable query and document sparsity. ## Results ### Headline Results (BEIR-15, nDCG@10) BEIR-15 scores are average nDCG@10 across 15 datasets, reported on a 0–100 scale. Sparse models use dot-product scoring and exact search over each full evaluation corpus. All rows use unpruned query and document vectors. Dense and late-interaction results are taken from our [DenseOn and LateOn blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon).

SlideOn achieves the highest BEIR-15 score among the sparse models below 3B parameters in this comparison. It improves on SPARSEUP by 2.22 points and on DenseOn by 0.48 points, while remaining 0.54 points behind LateOn. The figures below show how pruning changes the comparison when search and storage costs are taken into account. ### Retrieval Quality versus Search and Storage Cost Query pruning reduces the number of posting lists consulted during search. Document pruning shortens those lists and reduces the number of stored document weights. Matryoshka training concentrates retrieval information in the strongest latents so that both budgets can be adjusted after training.

Retrieval quality versus search cost for SlideOn and sub-2B baselines. Blue points show SlideOn with documents pruned to the top-512 latents and varying query budgets, where q-full denotes unpruned queries. Higher BEIR-15 ↑ scores and lower FLOPS ↓ are better. Retrieval FLOPS are measured on a subset of SciFact, NFCorpus, and FiQA.

Retrieval quality versus index storage cost for SlideOn and sub-2B baselines. Blue points show SlideOn with unpruned queries and varying document budgets, where d-full denotes unpruned documents. Higher BEIR-15 ↑ scores and lower NNZ ↓ are better. Document NNZ is measured on SciFact, NFCorpus, and FiQA.

Retrieval FLOPS estimates the expected number of shared active features per query–document pair. It is a search-cost proxy, not measured latency or encoder FLOPs. Document NNZ is the average number of nonzero document features and serves as a storage-cost proxy, rather than a measurement of index size in bytes. At 149M parameters it decisively beats `GTE-ModernBERT` (55.19) at the same size, and more tellingly outperforms `snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0` (55.22, 568M) and `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` (55.52, 595M) despite being roughly 4× smaller. DenseOn also stays within half a point of the strongest current-generation dense baselines, `pplx-embed-v1-0.6B` (56.70, 596M) and `jina-embeddings-v5-text-nano` (56.08, 239M), both substantially larger. ### Decontaminated BEIR (12 datasets, NDCG@10) Standard benchmarks risk overestimating model quality when training data overlaps with evaluation corpora. This is a non-negligible risk in our case, as our mixture explorations are mostly built on BEIR evaluation. To quantify this and ensure that our model has not memorized possible leakage, we built decontaminated versions of the BEIR datasets by removing samples found in both the mGTE training dataset and in our internal training datasets. Since many retrieval models draw from similar public sources (Wikipedia, MS MARCO, Common Crawl, academic corpora), we expect significant overlap across models and believe the decontaminated benchmarks provide a meaningful, if imperfect, stress test. The decontaminated datasets are publicly available on HuggingFace. Despite being in the toughest position (as the decontamination is based on our data), LateOn and DenseOn stay consistent under decontamination. LateOn keeps its #1 position and DenseOn stays in the top four (only falling behind our other strong multi-vector model, ColBERT-Zero). Neither model flinches, which is direct evidence of generalization rather than overfitting. More broadly, ColBERT models seems to generalize better under decontamination: all three ColBERT models hold or improve their ranking, and they take 2 of the top 3 decontaminated positions. Although DenseOn holds strong, some dense models are hit harder, for example `GTE-ModernBERT`, dropping from 8th to last, which is particularly interesting considering our base mixture is derived from theirs. This highlights the strength of our curation methodology. While other models such as `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` also drop some ranks, hinting at an overlap with the BEIR evaluation, it is worth noting that newer models, such as the new `jina-embeddings-v5` and `pplx-embed-v1-0.6b` seems to exhibit stronger evidence of generalization rather than overfitting.
## Related Checkpoints | Model | Stage | Link | |:---|:---|:---| | DenseOn *(this card)* | Pre-training + fine-tuning | [`lightonai/DenseOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn) | | DenseOn-unsupervised | Pre-training only | [`lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised) | | LateOn | Multi-vector counterpart | [`lightonai/LateOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn) | | LateOn-unsupervised | Multi-vector, pre-training only | [`lightonai/LateOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn-unsupervised) | ## Model Details ### Model Description - Model Type: Sentence Transformer - Base model: [DenseOn-unsupervised](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised) (ModernBERT-base) - Maximum Sequence Length: 512 tokens - Output Dimensionality: 768 dimensions - Similarity Function: Cosine Similarity - Pooling: CLS token - Prompts: `query:` for queries, `document:` for documents - Language: English - License: Apache 2.0 ### Model Sources - Documentation: [Sentence Transformers Documentation](https://sbert.net) - Repository: [Sentence Transformers on GitHub](https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers) - Hugging Face: [Sentence Transformers on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models?library=sentence-transformers) ### Full Model Architecture ``` SentenceTransformer( (0): Transformer({'max_seq_length': 512, 'do_lower_case': False, 'architecture': 'ModernBertModel'}) (1): Pooling({'word_embedding_dimension': 768, 'pooling_mode_cls_token': True, 'pooling_mode_mean_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_max_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_mean_sqrt_len_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_weightedmean_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_lasttoken': False, 'include_prompt': True}) ) ``` ## Usage ### Direct Usage (Sentence Transformers) First install the Sentence Transformers library: ```bash pip install -U sentence-transformers ``` Then you can load this model and run inference. ```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer # Download from the Hub model = SentenceTransformer("lightonai/DenseOn") # Run inference queries = [ "Which planet is known as the Red Planet?", ] documents = [ "Venus is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and proximity.", "Mars, known for its reddish appearance, is often referred to as the Red Planet.", "Saturn, famous for its rings, is sometimes mistaken for the Red Planet.", ] query_embeddings = model.encode(queries, prompt_name="query") document_embeddings = model.encode(documents, prompt_name="document") print(query_embeddings.shape, document_embeddings.shape) # [1, 768] [3, 768] # Get the similarity scores for the embeddings similarities = model.similarity(query_embeddings, document_embeddings) print(similarities) ``` ## Training Details ### Framework Versions - Python: 3.11.10 - Sentence Transformers: 5.1.1 - Transformers: 4.57.5 - PyTorch: 2.9.0+cu128 - Accelerate: 1.12.0 - Datasets: 3.6.0 - Tokenizers: 0.22.1 ## Citation ### BibTeX #### DenseOn and LateOn ```bibtex @misc{sourty2026denseonlateon, title={DenseOn with the LateOn: Open State-of-the-Art Single and Multi-Vector Models}, author={Sourty, Raphael and Chaffin, Antoine and Weller, Orion and Demoura, Paulo and Chatelain, Amelie}, year={2026}, howpublished={\url{https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon}}, } ``` #### PyLate ```bibtex @inproceedings{DBLP:conf/cikm/ChaffinS25, author = {Antoine Chaffin and Rapha{\"{e}}l Sourty}, editor = {Meeyoung Cha and Chanyoung Park and Noseong Park and Carl Yang and Senjuti Basu Roy and Jessie Li and Jaap Kamps and Kijung Shin and Bryan Hooi and Lifang He}, title = {PyLate: Flexible Training and Retrieval for Late Interaction Models}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the 34th {ACM} International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, {CIKM} 2025, Seoul, Republic of Korea, November 10-14, 2025}, pages = {6334--6339}, publisher = {{ACM}}, year = {2025}, url = {https://github.com/lightonai/pylate}, doi = {10.1145/3746252.3761608}, } ``` #### Sentence Transformers ```bibtex @inproceedings{reimers-2019-sentence-bert, title = "Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks", author = "Reimers, Nils and Gurevych, Iryna", booktitle = "Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing", month = "11", year = "2019", publisher = "Association for Computational Linguistics", url = "https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084" } ``` ## Acknowledgements We thank Xin Zhang, Zach Nussbaum, Tom Aarsen, Bo Wang, Eugene Yang, Benjamin Clavié, Nandan Thakur, Oskar Hallström and Iacopo Poli for their valuable contributions and feedback. [![Website](https://img.shields.io/badge/LightOn-Website-blue?logo=google-chrome)](https://lighton.ai) [![LinkedIn](https://img.shields.io/badge/LightOn-LinkedIn-0A66C2?logo=linkedin)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/lighton/) [![X](https://img.shields.io/badge/@LightOnIO-X-black?logo=x)](https://x.com/LightOnIO) 📚 [Collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/lightonai/mdenseon-and-mlateon) | 📝 [Multilingual Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon) | 📝 [English Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon) | 📝 [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27178)

mDenseOn

State-of-the-Art Multilingual Dense Retrieval Model by LightOn

mDenseOn | mLateOn | DenseOn | LateOn | PyLate | FastPlaid

> 🎯 TL;DR: A 307M-parameter multilingual dense (single-vector) retrieval model achieving state-of-the-art results across multilingual retrieval (MIRACL), long-document retrieval (MLDR), English general-domain retrieval (BEIR), and code retrieval (MTEB Code). Built by extending our validated open English data recipe to eight additional languages via translate-train, producing one of the largest open multilingual retrieval training sets to date (2.8B pairs). ## About the mDenseOn / mLateOn Family With [DenseOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn) and [LateOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn), we demonstrated that an open, carefully curated data recipe can match closed-data retrieval models on English. mDenseOn and mLateOn extend this recipe to multilingual, long-context, and code retrieval. Rather than independently collecting multilingual corpora from scratch (which would be expensive, uneven across languages, and hard to curate at the same quality), we applied the translate-train approach: machine-translating our validated English data into eight target languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Swedish, Norwegian, and Arabic) and adding cross-lingual pairs for cross-lingual alignment. For more information, please read our [multilingual models blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon), our [English models blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon) and our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27178). ## mDenseOn mDenseOn is a multilingual dense (single-vector) retrieval model built on mmBERT-base (307M parameters), trained by [LightOn](https://lighton.ai). It encodes queries and documents independently using cosine similarity with `query:`/`document:` prefixes and [CLS] pooling, supporting context lengths of up to 8,192 tokens. mDenseOn notably: - Achieves 56.70 NDCG@10 on BEIR, slightly surpassing the English-only DenseOn (56.20), confirming that multilingual capabilities do not come at the cost of English quality. - Reaches 59.61 on MIRACL target languages, competitive with similarly-sized models like EmbeddingGemma. - Scores 64.98 on MLDR target languages, competitive with most dense baselines - Achieves 71.53 on MTEB Code, the second-best sub-350M dense model, despite using only fine-tuning-stage code data and no code-specific pre-training. Alongside mDenseOn, we also trained [mLateOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn), a late-interaction variant using the same setup. mLateOn achieves substantially stronger results, especially on multilingual and long-context tasks, and generalizes to languages outside of the training set, effectively circumventing the main limitation of translate-train for dense models. If your use case permits multi-vector retrieval, we recommend mLateOn. See our [multilingual blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon) for full results and analysis. ## Results ### Headline Results (NDCG@10) MIRACLtgt and MLDRtgt include only the languages overlapping with our target languages; MIRACL and MLDR include all benchmark languages. | Model | Size | BEIR | MIRACLtgt | MIRACL | MLDRtgt | MLDR | Code | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Our models | | | | | | | | | mLateOn | 307M | 57.56 | 65.61 | 67.04 | 87.69 | 77.92 | 73.48 | | mDenseOn | 307M | 56.70 | 59.61 | 58.02 | 64.98 | 51.59 | 71.53 | | Dense baselines | | | | | | | | | pplx-embed-v1-0.6b | 596M | 56.70 | 63.18 | 68.20 | 57.08 | 43.98 | 75.18 | | jina-v5-text-small | 677M | 56.70 | 61.03 | 66.56 | 53.00 | 43.83 | 73.01 | | jina-v5-text-nano | 239M | 56.08 | 60.86 | 65.84 | 56.71 | 47.20 | 70.75 | | arctic-embed-l-v2 | 568M | 55.55 | 60.78 | 66.53 | 57.01 | 48.03 | 53.17 | | Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B | 596M | 55.33 | 57.64 | 60.62 | 59.11 | 50.06 | 73.75 | | harrier-oss-v1-0.6b | 596M | 55.04 | 57.41 | 63.68 | 53.84 | 44.23 | 70.97 | | harrier-oss-v1-270m | 268M | 50.82 | 48.95 | 57.11 | 52.31 | 42.63 | 63.79 | | embeddinggemma-300m | 308M | 53.69 | 58.72 | 64.58 | 49.11 | 40.89 | 68.81 | | gte-multilingual-base | 305M | 51.08 | 57.39 | 64.14 | 66.41 | 56.65 | 57.46 | | voyage-4-nano | 340M | 49.96 | 49.29 | 58.65 | 62.10 | 51.97 | 76.43 | | BGE-M3 | 568M | 48.78 | 62.22 | 69.62 | 61.16 | 52.47 | 51.49 | | granite-311m-r2 | 312M | 49.24 | 53.38 | 59.74 | 50.53 | 41.86 | 63.50 | | Late-interaction baselines | | | | | | | | | pplx-embed-v1-late-0.6b | 596M | 56.11 | 63.67 | 69.55 | 68.69 | 55.51 | 63.29 | | LFM2.5-ColBERT-350M | 353M | 54.50 | 57.40 | 42.45 | 78.39 | 61.05 | 51.62 | | jina-colbert-v2 | 559M | 52.96 | 62.19 | 65.65 | 13.97 | 11.54 | 49.88 | | GTE-ModernColBERT | 149M | 54.23 | 43.96 | 36.35 | 67.68 | 45.95 | 54.37 | | ColBERT-Zero | 149M | 55.82 | 43.89 | 39.36 | 71.32 | 49.50 | 53.59 | mDenseOn at 307M parameters is competitive with or outperforms models up to twice its size on most target-language axes. Among dense models of comparable size, it outperforms EmbeddingGemma and granite-311m-r2 on every target-language axis, and gte-multilingual-base on all but MLDR. ### Key Findings English quality improved. mDenseOn reaches 56.70 on BEIR, slightly surpassing the English-only DenseOn (56.20), confirming that multilingual training need not degrade English performance. Strong target-language performance. On the nine languages we translated into, mDenseOn is competitive with models trained on many more languages. Dense models generalize less to unseen languages. On the full MIRACL and MLDR benchmarks (which include languages not seen during retrieval training), mDenseOn drops noticeably. This is expected for single-vector models, whose compressed representation transfers less readily to languages absent from fine-tuning. For broader language coverage without exhaustive translation, consider [mLateOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn), which generalizes substantially better to unseen languages. Code retrieval from fine-tuning alone. mDenseOn scores 71.53 on MTEB Code using only fine-tuning-stage code data (from LateOn-Code), with no code-specific pre-training. Adding code data at pre-training time may yield further gains. ## Related Checkpoints | Model | Description | Link | |:---|:---|:---| | mDenseOn *(this card)* | Multilingual dense retriever (recommended for multilingual dense) | [`lightonai/mDenseOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mDenseOn) | | mDenseOn-unsupervised | Multilingual dense, pre-training only | [`lightonai/mDenseOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mDenseOn-unsupervised) | | mLateOn | Multilingual late-interaction retriever (strongest multilingual) | [`lightonai/mLateOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn) | | mLateOn-unsupervised | Multilingual late-interaction, pre-training only | [`lightonai/mLateOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn-unsupervised) | | DenseOn | English-only dense retriever | [`lightonai/DenseOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn) | | DenseOn-unsupervised | English-only dense, pre-training only | [`lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised) | | LateOn | English-only late-interaction retriever | [`lightonai/LateOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn) | | LateOn-unsupervised | English-only late-interaction, pre-training only | [`lightonai/LateOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn-unsupervised) | ## Training Data We release all datasets used to train our English and multilingual embedding models. ### Pre-training Data * [Multilingual pre-training curated data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/multilingual-embeddings-pre-training-curated) — 2.16B pairs * [English pre-training curated data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-pre-training-curated) — 665M pairs Together these form the 2.8B-pair ready-to-train pre-training mixture. The multilingual corpus spans the eight target languages and includes a 220M-pair cross-lingual split. The curated English corpus is built after filtering and deduplicating the raw English data. The complete 1.4B-pair annotated parent dataset is released as [English pre-training unfiltered data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-pre-training). ### Fine-tuning Data A ready-to-train fine-tuning mixture of 16.3M samples, filtered with NV-Retriever methodology to remove false negatives: any mined candidate scoring above 95% of the positive's relevance is discarded, and the top 10 surviving hard negatives are kept per sample. The mixture is then annotated with the [mxbai-rerank-large-v2](https://huggingface.co/mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2) cross-encoder for distillation. We release one dataset per language, plus two code splits: * [English](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-en) * [French](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-fr) * [Spanish](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-es) * [Italian](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-it) * [German](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-de) * [Portuguese](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-pt) * [Arabic](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-ar) * [Norwegian](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-no) * [Swedish](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-sv) * [Code](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-code) * [Code Edit](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-code-edit) Multilingual data. MIRACL and MLDR hard-negatives were mined directly in the available datasets with [snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0](https://huggingface.co/Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0) (2,048 mined negatives per sample) and the full unfiltered set is available at [embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered). All other splits follow the translate-train recipe: we apply the mentioned NV-Retriever filtering to the [English fine-tuning unfiltered data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning), then machine-translate the filtered samples into the eight target languages, carrying the original relevance scores. The unfiltered English fine-tuning parent corpus contains 1.88M examples with 2,048 mined negatives, scored with [GTE-ModernBERT](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base). Code data. The Code dataset is derived from [LateOn-Code data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/nv-embed-supervised-distill-dedup-code), where 2,048 negatives are mined with [GTE-ModernBERT](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base). The Code Edit dataset had no existing training set, so we built one from [CommitPackFT](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bigcode/commitpackft), decontaminated against the CodeEditSearch evaluation set by removing shared commit SHAs, exact normalized-text matches, and examples with ≥50% 13-gram containment overlap. Hard-negatives are likewise mined with GTE-ModernBERT, and its unfiltered mined set is released alongside the multilingual data in [embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered). For more information, please read our [multilingual blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon) and our [English blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon). Training scripts can be found [here](https://github.com/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon). ## Model Details ### Model Description - Model Type: Sentence Transformer - Base model: [mmBERT-base](https://huggingface.co/jhu-clsp/mmBERT-base) - Maximum Sequence Length: 8,192 tokens - Output Dimensionality: 768 dimensions - Similarity Function: Cosine Similarity - Pooling: [CLS] token - Prompts: `query:` for queries, `document:` for documents - Languages: English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Swedish, Norwegian, Arabic - License: Apache 2.0 ### Model Sources - Documentation: [Sentence Transformers Documentation](https://sbert.net) - Repository: [Sentence Transformers on GitHub](https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers) - Hugging Face: [Sentence Transformers on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models?library=sentence-transformers) ### Full Model Architecture ``` SentenceTransformer( (0): Transformer({'max_seq_length': 8192, 'do_lower_case': False, 'architecture': 'ModernBertModel'}) (1): Pooling({'word_embedding_dimension': 768, 'pooling_mode_cls_token': True, 'pooling_mode_mean_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_max_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_mean_sqrt_len_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_weightedmean_tokens': False, 'pooling_mode_lasttoken': False, 'include_prompt': True}) ) ``` ## Usage ### Direct Usage (Sentence Transformers) First install the Sentence Transformers library: ```bash pip install -U sentence-transformers ``` Then you can load this model and run inference. ```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer # Download from the Hub model = SentenceTransformer("lightonai/mDenseOn") # Run inference with multilingual queries and documents queries = [ "Quelle planète est connue comme la planète rouge ?", "Which planet is known as the Red Planet?", ] documents = [ "Venus wird oft als Zwilling der Erde bezeichnet wegen ihrer ähnlichen Größe.", "Mars, connu pour son apparence rougeâtre, est souvent appelé la planète rouge.", "Marte, conocido por su apariencia rojiza, es a menudo llamado el Planeta Rojo.", "Mars, known for its reddish appearance, is often referred to as the Red Planet.", ] query_embeddings = model.encode(queries, prompt_name="query") document_embeddings = model.encode(documents, prompt_name="document") print(query_embeddings.shape, document_embeddings.shape) # [2, 768] [4, 768] # Get the similarity scores for the embeddings similarities = model.similarity(query_embeddings, document_embeddings) print(similarities) ``` ### Framework Versions - Python: 3.11.10 - Sentence Transformers: 5.1.1 - Transformers: 4.57.5 - PyTorch: 2.9.0+cu128 - Accelerate: 1.12.0 - Datasets: 3.6.0 - Tokenizers: 0.22.1 ## mLateOn

State-of-the-Art Multilingual ColBERT Retrieval Model by LightOn

mDenseOn | mLateOn | DenseOn | LateOn | PyLate | FastPlaid

> 🎯 TL;DR: A 307M-parameter multilingual ColBERT (multi-vector) retrieval model achieving state-of-the-art results across multilingual retrieval (MIRACL), long-document retrieval (MLDR), English general-domain retrieval (BEIR), and code retrieval (MTEB Code). Trained on nine languages only, yet generalizes to unseen languages and scripts, demonstrating that late interaction enables translate-train viability for broad multilingual coverage without exhaustive translation. ## About the mDenseOn / mLateOn Family With [DenseOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn) and [LateOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn), we demonstrated that an open, carefully curated data recipe can match closed-data retrieval models on English. mDenseOn and mLateOn extend this recipe to multilingual, long-context, and code retrieval. Rather than independently collecting multilingual corpora from scratch (which would be expensive, uneven across languages, and hard to curate at the same quality), we applied the translate-train approach: machine-translating our validated English data into eight target languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Swedish, Norwegian, and Arabic) and adding cross-lingual pairs for cross-lingual alignment. For more information, please read our [multilingual models blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon), our [English models blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon) and our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27178). ## mLateOn mLateOn is a multilingual ColBERT (multi-vector) retrieval model built on mmBERT-base (307M parameters), trained by [LightOn](https://lighton.ai) using [PyLate](https://github.com/lightonai/pylate). It supports context lengths of up to 8,192 tokens for documents and queries, using MaxSim scoring. mLateOn notably: - Achieves the highest BEIR score among all evaluated models at 57.56 NDCG@10, surpassing even the English-only LateOn (57.22) and dense baselines up to twice its size, showing that multilingual training can actually *improve* English performance. - Leads all models on MIRACL target languages at 65.61, and remains competitive on the full benchmark (67.04) despite being trained on only nine languages, outperforming most models trained on many more languages. - Opens a massive gap on MLDR at 87.69 on target languages, more than 9 points ahead of the next-best model (LFM2.5-ColBERT-350M at 78.39), combining the multilingual generalization of late interaction with ColBERT's affinity for long-context retrieval. - Generalizes to unseen languages, including scripts not seen during retrieval training (Cyrillic, Japanese, etc), demonstrating that multi-vector representations can transfer to languages absent from retrieval training. - Achieves strong code retrieval at 73.48 on MTEB Code, using only fine-tuning-stage code data. Perhaps the most important finding: the translate-train recipe applied to a dense encoder produces limited generalization beyond target languages, but applying it to a late-interaction architecture lifts this restriction. With mLateOn, you don't need to exhaustively translate to all target languages, a handful of representative languages is sufficient for broad multilingual coverage. Alongside mLateOn, we also trained [mDenseOn](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mDenseOn), a dense (single-vector) variant using the same setup. If your setup does not allow multi-vector, mDenseOn is a strong single-vector alternative, but trades off generalization to unseen languages and long-context performance. See our [multilingual blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon) for full results and analysis. ## Results ### Headline Results (NDCG@10) MIRACLtgt and MLDRtgt include only the languages overlapping with our target languages; MIRACL and MLDR include all benchmark languages. | Model | Size | BEIR | MIRACLtgt | MIRACL | MLDRtgt | MLDR | Code | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Our models | | | | | | | | | mLateOn | 307M | 57.56 | 65.61 | 67.04 | 87.69 | 77.92 | 73.48 | | mDenseOn | 307M | 56.70 | 59.61 | 58.02 | 64.98 | 51.59 | 71.53 | | Dense baselines | | | | | | | | | pplx-embed-v1-0.6b | 596M | 56.70 | 63.18 | 68.20 | 57.08 | 43.98 | 75.18 | | jina-v5-text-small | 677M | 56.70 | 61.03 | 66.56 | 53.00 | 43.83 | 73.01 | | jina-v5-text-nano | 239M | 56.08 | 60.86 | 65.84 | 56.71 | 47.20 | 70.75 | | arctic-embed-l-v2 | 568M | 55.55 | 60.78 | 66.53 | 57.01 | 48.03 | 53.17 | | Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B | 596M | 55.33 | 57.64 | 60.62 | 59.11 | 50.06 | 73.75 | | harrier-oss-v1-0.6b | 596M | 55.04 | 57.41 | 63.68 | 53.84 | 44.23 | 70.97 | | harrier-oss-v1-270m | 268M | 50.82 | 48.95 | 57.11 | 52.31 | 42.63 | 63.79 | | embeddinggemma-300m | 308M | 53.69 | 58.72 | 64.58 | 49.11 | 40.89 | 68.81 | | gte-multilingual-base | 305M | 51.08 | 57.39 | 64.14 | 66.41 | 56.65 | 57.46 | | voyage-4-nano | 340M | 49.96 | 49.29 | 58.65 | 62.10 | 51.97 | 76.43 | | BGE-M3 | 568M | 48.78 | 62.22 | 69.62 | 61.16 | 52.47 | 51.49 | | granite-311m-r2 | 312M | 49.24 | 53.38 | 59.74 | 50.53 | 41.86 | 63.50 | | Late-interaction baselines | | | | | | | | | pplx-embed-v1-late-0.6b | 596M | 56.11 | 63.67 | 69.55 | 68.69 | 55.51 | 63.29 | | LFM2.5-ColBERT-350M | 353M | 54.50 | 57.40 | 42.45 | 78.39 | 61.05 | 51.62 | | jina-colbert-v2 | 559M | 52.96 | 62.19 | 65.65 | 13.97 | 11.54 | 49.88 | | GTE-ModernColBERT | 149M | 54.23 | 43.96 | 36.35 | 67.68 | 45.95 | 54.37 | | ColBERT-Zero | 149M | 55.82 | 43.89 | 39.36 | 71.32 | 49.50 | 53.59 | ### Key Findings English quality improved. mLateOn reaches 57.56 on BEIR, *higher* than the English-only LateOn (57.22). Multilingual training does not degrade English performance; it can enhance it. Strongest multilingual retrieval on target languages. mLateOn leads all models at 65.61 on MIRACL target languages, ahead of pplx-embed-v1-late-0.6b (63.67) and bge-m3 (62.22), both roughly twice its size and trained on substantially more languages. Exceptional long-document retrieval. On MLDR target languages, mLateOn achieves 87.69, a gap of around 9 points over the next-best model. This advantage stems from two complementary sources: the stronger multilingual generalization of late interaction, and ColBERT-style models' well-documented affinity for long-context retrieval, where fine-grained token-level matching exploits longer documents more effectively than a single pooled vector. Late interaction generalizes beyond the retrieval-training languages. On the full MIRACL, mLateOn actually gains from target to full (67.04 vs. 65.61), highlighting exceptional performance on languages never seen during retrieval training. This is in contrast to mDenseOn, which drops about 1.6 points. Even though we trained mostly on Romance languages (plus Arabic), we observe very strong performance on other scripts such as Cyrillic and Japanese. For practitioners: with a late-interaction model, you don't need to exhaustively translate to all target languages. Translating to a handful of representative languages is sufficient for strong multilingual coverage. ## Related Checkpoints | Model | Description | Link | |:---|:---|:---| | mLateOn *(this card)* | Multilingual late-interaction retriever (strongest multilingual) | [`lightonai/mLateOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn) | | mLateOn-unsupervised | Multilingual late-interaction, pre-training only | [`lightonai/mLateOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mLateOn-unsupervised) | | mDenseOn | Multilingual dense retriever | [`lightonai/mDenseOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mDenseOn) | | mDenseOn-unsupervised | Multilingual dense, pre-training only | [`lightonai/mDenseOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/mDenseOn-unsupervised) | | LateOn | English-only late-interaction retriever | [`lightonai/LateOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn) | | LateOn-unsupervised | English-only late-interaction, pre-training only | [`lightonai/LateOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LateOn-unsupervised) | | DenseOn | English-only dense retriever | [`lightonai/DenseOn`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn) | | DenseOn-unsupervised | English-only dense, pre-training only | [`lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised`](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/DenseOn-unsupervised) | ## Training Data We release all datasets used to train our English and multilingual embedding models. ### Pre-training Data * [Multilingual pre-training curated data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/multilingual-embeddings-pre-training-curated) — 2.16B pairs * [English pre-training curated data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-pre-training-curated) — 665M pairs Together these form the 2.8B-pair ready-to-train pre-training mixture. The multilingual corpus spans the eight target languages and includes a 220M-pair cross-lingual split. The curated English corpus is built after filtering and deduplicating the raw English data. The complete 1.4B-pair annotated parent dataset is released as [English pre-training unfiltered data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-pre-training). ### Fine-tuning Data A ready-to-train fine-tuning mixture of 16.3M samples, filtered with NV-Retriever methodology to remove false negatives: any mined candidate scoring above 95% of the positive's relevance is discarded, and the top 10 surviving hard negatives are kept per sample. The mixture is then annotated with the [mxbai-rerank-large-v2](https://huggingface.co/mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2) cross-encoder for distillation. We release one dataset per language, plus two code splits: * [English](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-en) * [French](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-fr) * [Spanish](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-es) * [Italian](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-it) * [German](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-de) * [Portuguese](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-pt) * [Arabic](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-ar) * [Norwegian](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-no) * [Swedish](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-sv) * [Code](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-code) * [Code Edit](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-filtered-code-edit) Multilingual data. MIRACL and MLDR hard-negatives were mined directly in the available datasets with [snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0](https://huggingface.co/Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0) (2,048 mined negatives per sample) and the full unfiltered set is available at [embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered). All other splits follow the translate-train recipe: we apply the mentioned NV-Retriever filtering to the [English fine-tuning unfiltered data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning), then machine-translate the filtered samples into the eight target languages, carrying the original relevance scores. The unfiltered English fine-tuning parent corpus contains 1.88M examples with 2,048 mined negatives, scored with [GTE-ModernBERT](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base). Code data. The Code dataset is derived from [LateOn-Code data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/nv-embed-supervised-distill-dedup-code), where 2,048 negatives are mined with [GTE-ModernBERT](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base). The Code Edit dataset had no existing training set, so we built one from [CommitPackFT](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bigcode/commitpackft), decontaminated against the CodeEditSearch evaluation set by removing shared commit SHAs, exact normalized-text matches, and examples with ≥50% 13-gram containment overlap. Hard-negatives are likewise mined with GTE-ModernBERT, and its unfiltered mined set is released alongside the multilingual data in [embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning-multilingual-unfiltered). For more information, please read our [multilingual blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon) and our [English blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/lightonai/denseon-lateon). Training scripts can be found [here](https://github.com/lightonai/mdenseon-mlateon). ## Model Details ### Model Description - Model Type: PyLate ColBERT model - Base model: [mmBERT-base](https://huggingface.co/jhu-clsp/mmBERT-base) - Query/Document Length: 8,192 tokens - Output Dimensionality: 128 dimensions - Similarity Function: MaxSim - Languages: English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Swedish, Norwegian, Arabic - License: Apache 2.0 ### Model Sources - Documentation: [PyLate Documentation](https://lightonai.github.io/pylate/) - Repository: [PyLate on GitHub](https://github.com/lightonai/pylate) - Hugging Face: [PyLate models on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models?library=PyLate) ### Full Model Architecture ``` ColBERT( (0): Transformer({'max_seq_length': 8192, 'do_lower_case': False, 'architecture': 'ModernBertModel'}) (1): Dense({'in_features': 768, 'out_features': 1536, 'bias': False, 'activation_function': 'torch.nn.modules.linear.Identity', 'use_residual': True}) (2): Dense({'in_features': 1536, 'out_features': 768, 'bias': False, 'activation_function': 'torch.nn.modules.linear.Identity', 'use_residual': True}) (3): Dense({'in_features': 768, 'out_features': 128, 'bias': False, 'activation_function': 'torch.nn.modules.linear.Identity', 'use_residual': False}) ) ``` ## Usage ### Sentence Transformers This model can be used with [Sentence Transformers](https://www.sbert.net/) as a multi-vector (ColBERT-style late interaction) retriever via the `MultiVectorEncoder`: ```bash pip install "sentence-transformers>=6.0.0" ``` ```python from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder model = MultiVectorEncoder("lightonai/mLateOn") query = "Which planet is the Red Planet?" documents = [ "Mars, known for its reddish appearance, is often referred to as the Red Planet.", "Mars, connu pour son apparence rougeâtre, est souvent appelé la planète rouge.", "Mars, bekannt für sein rötliches Erscheinungsbild, wird oft als der Rote Planet bezeichnet.", "Venus is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and proximity.", ] query_embeddings = model.encode_query(query) document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents) print(query_embeddings.shape, document_embeddings[0].shape) # (10, 128) (20, 128) # MaxSim late-interaction scoring (higher is more relevant) scores = model.similarity(query_embeddings, document_embeddings) print(scores) # tensor([[9.6029, 9.5838, 9.5877, 9.4578]]) ``` ### PyLate First install the PyLate library: ```bash pip install -U pylate ``` ### Retrieval Use this model with PyLate to index and retrieve documents. The index uses [FastPlaid](https://github.com/lightonai/fast-plaid) for efficient similarity search. #### Indexing documents Load the ColBERT model and initialize the PLAID index, then encode and index your documents: ```python from pylate import indexes, models, retrieve # Step 1: Load the ColBERT model model = models.ColBERT( model_name_or_path="lightonai/mLateOn", ) # Step 2: Initialize the PLAID index index = indexes.PLAID( index_folder="pylate-index", index_name="index", override=True, # This overwrites the existing index if any ) # Step 3: Encode the documents (supports multilingual content) documents_ids = ["1", "2", "3", "4"] documents = [ "Mars, known for its reddish appearance, is often referred to as the Red Planet.", "Mars, connu pour son apparence rougeâtre, est souvent appelé la planète rouge.", "Mars, bekannt für sein rötliches Erscheinungsbild, wird oft als der Rote Planet bezeichnet.", "Venus is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and proximity.", ] documents_embeddings = model.encode( documents, batch_size=32, is_query=False, # Ensure that it is set to False to indicate that these are documents, not queries show_progress_bar=True, ) # Step 4: Add document embeddings to the index by providing embeddings and corresponding ids index.add_documents( documents_ids=documents_ids, documents_embeddings=documents_embeddings, ) ``` Note that you do not have to recreate the index and encode the documents every time. Once you have created an index and added the documents, you can re-use the index later by loading it: ```python # To load an index, simply instantiate it with the correct folder/name and without overriding it index = indexes.PLAID( index_folder="pylate-index", index_name="index", ) ``` #### Retrieving top-k documents for queries Once the documents are indexed, you can retrieve the top-k most relevant documents for a given set of queries — including cross-lingual retrieval: ```python # Step 1: Initialize the ColBERT retriever retriever = retrieve.ColBERT(index=index) # Step 2: Encode the queries (can be in any supported language) queries_embeddings = model.encode( [ "Quelle planète est connue comme la planète rouge ?", # French query "Which planet is the Red Planet?", # English query ], batch_size=32, is_query=True, # Ensure that it is set to True to indicate that these are queries show_progress_bar=True, ) # Step 3: Retrieve top-k documents (returns matches across all languages) scores = retriever.retrieve( queries_embeddings=queries_embeddings, k=10, # Retrieve the top 10 matches for each query ) ``` ### Reranking If you only want to use the ColBERT model to perform reranking on top of your first-stage retrieval pipeline without building an index, you can simply use the rank function and pass the queries and documents to rerank: ```python from pylate import rank, models queries = [ "Quelle planète est la planète rouge ?", "What is the largest planet in the solar system?", ] documents = [ ["Mars ist der Rote Planet.", "Venus ist der Zwilling der Erde."], ["Jupiter is the largest planet.", "Saturn is known for its rings.", "Mars is the Red Planet."], ] documents_ids = [ [1, 2], [1, 3, 2], ] model = models.ColBERT( model_name_or_path="lightonai/mLateOn", ) queries_embeddings = model.encode( queries, is_query=True, ) documents_embeddings = model.encode( documents, is_query=False, ) reranked_documents = rank.rerank( documents_ids=documents_ids, queries_embeddings=queries_embeddings, documents_embeddings=documents_embeddings, ) ``` ### Framework Versions - Python: 3.11.10 - Sentence Transformers: 5.1.1 - PyLate: 1.3.4 - Transformers: 4.57.5 - PyTorch: 2.9.0+cu128 - Accelerate: 1.12.0 - Datasets: 3.6.0 - Tokenizers: 0.22.1 ## Citation ### BibTeX #### mDenseOn and mLateOn ```bibtex Antoine Chaffin and Paulo Roberto Moura Junior and Amélie Chatelain}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2607.27178}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.CL}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27178}, } Li and Jaap Kamps and Kijung Shin and Bryan Hooi and Lifang He}, title = {PyLate: Flexible Training and Retrieval for Late Interaction Models}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the 34th {ACM} International "11", year = "2019", publisher = "Association for Computational Linguistics", url = "https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084" } ``` ## Acknowledgements We thank Eugene Yang for his feedback on adapting our
